title: Ramp-and-Stabilize Reservation Controller - PRD Notes
body:
Context / why this doc exists:

We keep getting TOIL and flakiness for customers that have unpredictable traffic spikes around batchy background jobs + interactive user flows. Current dedicated capacity designs provide reservation + burst credits, but we need a lighter-weight controller that focuses on three practical goals: smooth ramp-up (avoid sudden oversubscribe), short-term stabilized burst windows (give apps breathing room for microspikes), and clear isolation semantics when capacity is constrained.

This doc is a working PRD for a "Ramp-and-Stabilize Reservation Controller" (R-S Controller) — a policy layer that sits in the Dedicated capacity broker to manage transient capacity adjustments and tenant isolation during surges. Think of it as a low-latency advisor + enforcer: it mints short-lived reservation boosts subject to stabilization rules and isolation fences.

Goals (high level):
- Reduce noisy-neighbor incidents during microbursts by smoothing short-lived capacity allocation changes.
- Preserve SLAs for committed reservations while allowing controlled, observable bursts for opportunistic traffic.
- Make burst behavior explicit and predictable for customers (metrics, dashboards, failure modes).
- Keep operator runbooks simple: fast diagnosis, clear mitigation levers.

Non-goals:
- This is not a full predictive autoscaler that replaces forecasting/autopilot. It handles short horizon (seconds->minutes) stabilizing behavior only.
- Not intended to change long-term reservation pricing or commitment model.

Key concepts / terminology (working):
- Ramp window: a short window (configurable, default 45s) over which newly allocated burst capacity is gradually admitted to avoid sudden oversubscribe.
- Stabilization hold: after a burst boost is granted, we hold the effective capacity at the granted level for a minimum time (e.g., 120s) before allowing decay, to avoid churn.
- Burst escrow / burst tokens: a per-tenant credit bucket representing their short-term burst allowance. Tokens refill on schedule and can be lent/borrowed under policy.
- Isolation fence: enforced soft-limit that drops or reroutes best-effort traffic when cross-tenant interference risk exceeds threshold.
- Emergency tranche: small reserved buffer used only when critical system-level SLOs are at risk; requires operator confirmation to spend more than X%.

User stories / acceptance criteria:
- As a tenant with a committed pool, I want my critical routes to remain within latency SLOs even if another tenant spikes, unless they hit explicit hard isolation thresholds. (Acceptance: <2% p95 latency regressions for committed routes during bounded bursts.)
- As an admin, I want to see a time-series of ramp admission, token spend, and isolation events for every pool so I can debug incidents quickly. (Acceptance: metrics + trace links appear in Console within 30s of events.)
- As an app owner, I want to opt-in to a faster ramp policy for short jobs (low-latency tolerance) and a conservative ramp for interactive production. (Acceptance: flag-based policy selector per-tenant + per-route.)

Design proposal (core flows):
1) Admission flow when a new request arrives: check committed capacity -> if exceeded, consult burst tokens -> if tokens available, propose "temporary admission" tracked in a local admission log -> apply ramp gating (admitted fraction grows linearly over ramp window) -> return decision to broker/routing layer.
2) Stabilization: once admitted, mark allocations with a stability expiry. Eviction within the hold period allowed only for emergency tranche or explicit preemption policy.
3) Token mechanics: tokens earned via unused reservation carryover (configurable percent) + periodic top-ups. Tokens decay on use. Excess spending above tokens triggers isolation fences or rate-limited grace borrowing from emergency tranche.
4) Isolation detection: cross-tenant interference is measured by pool-level SLO breach delta (e.g., 5x increase in tail latency or CPU/GPU utilization spike beyond configured headroom). When detection triggers, the controller initiates graded responses: first soft limit (best-effort degrade), then lane-based throttles (non-critical routes), then tenant-level soft-isolation (no more bursts), finally emergency preemption if system SLOs endangered.

Policy knobs (exposed to config/Console):
- ramp_window_seconds (default 45s)
- stabilization_hold_seconds (default 120s)
- token_refill_rate and max_burst_token_cap
- emergency_tranche_pct_of_pool (default 3%)
- isolation_thresholds (latency delta, util pct, error-rate bump)
- policy_selector (conservative | balanced | aggressive) per-tenant/per-route

Operational considerations and metrics:
- Metrics to emit: ramp_admit_rate, tokens_spent, tokens_balance, stabilization_evictions, isolation_events (with categories), emergency_tranche_consumed, per-tenant p50/p95/p99 latency deltas during events.
- Logs: admission trace with request_id, tenant, route, decision path, timestamp. Keep traces for 7 days by default.
- Alerts: isolation_event_count > 3 in 5m for a pool -> page on-call SRE; emergency_tranche_consumed > 80% -> notify infra-ops.

Runbook snippet (incident triage):
- Symptoms: sudden p95 jump or large token spend across multiple tenants.
- Quick check: console -> pool dashboard -> ramp_admit_rate and tokens_spent timeline. Identify tenant(s) consuming tokens.
- Action 1: toggle policy_selector to conservative for noisy tenant(s) (Console toggle); monitor 60s.
- Action 2: if system SLOs still at risk, enable temporary emergency_tranche_lockdown (blocks further borrowing) and start scale up of Dedicated pool (if autoscale allowed).
- Postmortem: annotate event with root cause and whether ramp_window or token caps should be tuned.

Implementation notes (engineering constraints):
- Controller should be ownerless and horizontally scalable; state is small per-tenant and can live in existing capacity DB with optimistic updates. Avoid per-request remote calls in the hot path; use local caches refreshed periodically (<=5s staleness) and a lightweight admission RPC only for edge cases.
- Prefer deterministic admission decisions in a single region to avoid split-brain admissions. Cross-region routing falls back to region-stable behavior.
- We must account for model-specific resource signals (KV cache pressure, decoding loops) as they affect util->latency mapping. Hook into serving-runtime telemetry where possible.

Open questions / tradeoffs (items to resolve in next week):
- Ramp window vs. user-perceived latency: how conservative should defaults be for chat-first customers? (Affects p50 vs p99 differently)
- Token economics: should unused reservation always contribute or only the delta since last month? Implications for billing and customer expectations.
- Emergency tranche governance: automated use vs. operator approval. Simpler UX favors automation; safety favors operator gate.
- UX surfaces: how much detail do we expose in Console by default vs. a developer-only debug view?

Next steps / immediate TODOs:
- Sync with SRE and serving-runtime to finalize isolation detection signals (RDW-2145 owner: Priya).
- PoC: lightweight token bucket + ramp admission simulator using historical pool traces (owner: Miguel). Target 2-week spike sim.
- UX: Console mock for policy toggles and token charts (owner: Asha).
- Legal/pricing: confirm whether token carryover needs billing disclosure (ask finance).

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Consider a "soft warm start" where ramp admission is weighted by route priority rather than tenant-level only. Useful for multi-tenant apps with predictable critical vs. batch routes.
- Could pair with Optimize's workload profile to auto-suggest token caps.

- infra PR 678: admission-cache-implementation (prototype)

END - draft notes. This is intentionally a working doc; text will be reorganized into a formal PRD after PoC results.
